# Two Main Limitations on the IBM 1401

According to the essay, the two main limitations were:

1. **No input data available**: The only form of input to programs was data stored on punched cards, and Paul Graham didn't have any data stored on punched cards.

2. **Limited computational scope**: The only alternative was to write programs that didn't rely on input, such as calculating approximations of pi, but he didn't know enough math to do anything interesting with that approach.

**Effect on his accomplishments**: These limitations meant he couldn't write meaningful programs. As he states, "I can't remember any programs I wrote, because they can't have done much." The constraints essentially prevented him from creating anything substantive on that machine.

retrievalContext: I wrote what beginning writers were supposed to write then, and probably still are: short stories. My stories were awful. They had hardly any plot, just characters with strong feelings, which I imagined made them deep. The first programs I tried writing were on the IBM 1401 that our school district used for what was then called "data processing." This was in 9th grade, so I was 13 or 14. The school district's 1401 happened to be in the basement of our junior high school, and my friend Rich Draves and I got permission to use it. It was like a mini Bond villain's lair down there, with all these alien-looking machines — CPU, disk drives, printer, card reader — sitting up on a raised floor under bright fluorescent lights. The language we used was an early version of Fortran. You had to type programs on punch cards, then stack them in the card reader and press a button to load the program into memory and run it. The result would ordinarily be to print something on the spectacularly loud printer. I was puzzled by the 1401. I couldn't figure out what to do with it.

And in retrospect there's not much I could have done with it. The only form of input to programs was data stored on punched cards, and I didn't have any data stored on punched cards. The only other option was to do things that didn't rely on any input, like calculate approximations of pi, but I didn't know enough math to do anything interesting of that type. So I'm not surprised I can't remember any programs I wrote, because they can't have done much. My clearest memory is of the moment I learned it was possible for programs not to terminate, when one of mine didn't. On a machine without time-sharing, this was a social as well as a technical error, as the data center manager's expression made clear. With microcomputers, everything changed. Now you could have a computer sitting right in front of you, on a desk, that could respond to your keystrokes as it was running instead of just churning through a stack of punch cards and then stopping. [1]

The first of my friends to get a microcomputer built it himself. It was sold as a kit by Heathkit. I remember vividly how impressed and envious I felt watching him sitting in front of it, typing programs right into the computer. Computers were expensive in those days and it took me years of nagging before I convinced my father to buy one, a TRS-80, in about 1980. The gold standard then was the Apple II, but a TRS-80 was good enough. This was when I really started programming. I wrote simple games, a program to predict how high my model rockets would fly, and a word processor that my father used to write at least one book. There was only room in memory for about 2 pages of text, so he'd write 2 pages at a time and then print them out, but it was a lot better than a typewriter. Though I liked programming, I didn't plan to study it in college.

I realize that sounds rather wimpy. But attention is a zero sum game. If you can choose what to work on, and you choose a project that's not the best one (or at least a good one) for you, then it's getting in the way of another project that is. And at 50 there was some opportunity cost to screwing around. I started writing essays again, and wrote a bunch of new ones over the next few months. I even wrote a couple that weren't about startups. Then in March 2015 I started working on Lisp again. The distinctive thing about Lisp is that its core is a language defined by writing an interpreter in itself. It wasn't originally intended as a programming language in the ordinary sense. It was meant to be a formal model of computation, an alternative to the Turing machine. If you want to write an interpreter for a language in itself, what's the minimum set of predefined operators you need? The Lisp that John McCarthy invented, or more accurately discovered, is an answer to that question. [19]

McCarthy didn't realize this Lisp could even be used to program computers till his grad student Steve Russell suggested it. Russell translated McCarthy's interpreter into IBM 704 machine language, and from that point Lisp started also to be a programming language in the ordinary sense. But its origins as a model of computation gave it a power and elegance that other languages couldn't match. It was this that attracted me in college, though I didn't understand why at the time. McCarthy's 1960 Lisp did nothing more than interpret Lisp expressions. It was missing a lot of things you'd want in a programming language. So these had to be added, and when they were, they weren't defined using McCarthy's original axiomatic approach. That wouldn't have been feasible at the time. McCarthy tested his interpreter by hand-simulating the execution of programs. But it was already getting close to the limit of interpreters you could test that way — indeed, there was a bug in it that McCarthy had overlooked. And as long as every change you made to McCarthy's Lisp was a discoveredness-preserving transformation, you could, in principle, end up with a complete language that had this quality. Harder to do than to talk about, of course, but if it was possible in principle, why not try?

# Paul Graham's Reasoning for Switching from Philosophy to AI

Based on the essay, Paul Graham's decision to switch from philosophy to AI was driven by his disappointing discovery about what philosophy actually offered as a field of study.

## His Initial Expectations vs. Reality

Graham initially believed philosophy was "the study of the ultimate truths, compared to which the things studied in other fields would be mere domain knowledge." However, when he arrived at college, he discovered this was not the case.

## What He Found Instead

He discovered that **other fields took up so much of the space of ideas that there wasn't much left for these supposed ultimate truths.** As he puts it: "All that seemed left for philosophy were edge cases that people in other fields felt could safely be ignored."

In other words, philosophy had been reduced to addressing only the peripheral questions and problems that other disciplines didn't consider important enough to tackle.

## The Practical Outcome

Rather than continue with a field that felt intellectually limiting, Graham made a pragmatic decision: "I kept taking philosophy courses and they kept being boring. So I decided to switch to AI."

His switch to AI was motivated by two specific inspirations: a Heinlein novel featuring an intelligent computer and a PBS documentary demonstrating Terry Winograd's SHRDLU program—both of which made AI seem like an exciting and imminent frontier.

I had gotten into a program at Cornell that didn't make you choose a major. You could take whatever classes you liked, and choose whatever you liked to put on your degree. testCases.input: Paul Graham initially pursued AI in graduate school but eventually realized that the AI approaches being practiced at the time were fundamentally flawed. Explain what Graham identified as the core problem with the AI methods of that era, and describe how this realization led him to change his academic focus.
testCases.actualOutput:
# Graham's Critique of 1980s AI and His Pivot

## The Core Problem

Graham identified that the AI methods of his era—which used explicit data structures to represent concepts and formal language parsing—were fundamentally limited. While programs like SHRDLU could handle a narrow subset of natural language by translating it into formal representations, this approach created **"an unbridgeable gap between what they could do and actually understanding natural language."** He realized it was not simply a matter of teaching the program more words; the entire methodology was broken and could never achieve true intelligence like the computer "Mike" he had envisioned.

## His Academic Pivot

Rather than abandon computer science entirely, Graham looked for what he could "salvage from the wreckage of [his] plans." He discovered that **Lisp itself was intellectually interesting independent of AI**, even though most people valued it primarily for AI applications. 

Graham therefore shifted his focus from AI to **Lisp programming**, eventually deciding to write a book about Lisp hacking—*On Lisp*—which he began during graduate school and published in 1993. This reorientation proved productive, as writing about the subject helped him develop deep expertise in the language.
